case_title: Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and Others v. State of Karnataka
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute: alleged grudge by the accused over the murder of a relative of accused A-4 two years earlier, in which the victim's family members were arraigned
statutory_provisions: IPC s.143, s.147, s.148, s.506(2), s.302 r/w s.149 (charged); High Court convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34; Supreme Court also examined Evidence Act s.27 and s.60
weapon: Jambiya (jambai), axes, sickles and a koyta (as alleged; recovered weapons held not proved)
evidence_type: Eyewitness testimony (PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW-4, PW-5, PW-6, PW-15; found unreliable or contradictory); medical evidence (PW-17); recovery and disclosure evidence (PW-27; rejected); FIR/complaint (Ex P-10; treated as post-investigation document)
confession: Section 27 disclosure statements of A-1 and A-2 (Ex P-15, P-16) and voluntary statement of A-3 were not proved and were not relied on
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted all six accused (A-1 to A-6) on 23 July 2005; no sentence
high_court_outcome: State's appeal allowed in part; acquittal of A-1, A-2 and A-3 reversed; convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 50,000 each (default two years); appeals against A-5 and A-6 dismissed; appeal against A-4 abated
neutral_facts: The victim's father owned agricultural land and a house in a village. In the morning of a September day in 2001, the victim went with four farm workers to build a check dam on the family land. The father packed their lunch at midday and visited the field. Work stopped at about 3.30 pm, and the group set off for the village. Near a particular landholding at about 4 pm, several accused allegedly appeared and said that the victim's side had killed a member of their family and that they would take revenge in the same manner. The accused were said to be armed with a jambiya, axes and sickles, and the victim was beaten and fell. The father alleged that he was threatened and hid in bushes until after sunset. He then returned home and told family members. A written complaint was lodged at the police station early the next morning, and an FIR was registered. Investigation led to a charge sheet against the accused and others. Twenty-seven witnesses were examined. Four workers and the father were presented as eyewitnesses, along with another witness. The medical jurist described decomposition of the body and an estimated time of death more than 24 hours before autopsy. Witnesses said it had rained heavily for about three days before the incident. The investigating officer described recoveries of axes, a koyta, a jambiya and sickles made on the basis of statements of the accused. The complainant said police showed him the weapons on the day of the incident. No serological opinion on the weapons was obtained.
physical_harm: Death of the victim after being belaboured with weapons (as alleged); the Court noted that only the deceased was injured
motive: alleged: revenge for the murder of the son of accused A-4 two years earlier; the Court found this motive too remote to impute to the accused and noted it could equally be a motive for false implication
key_evidence_accepted: No incriminating evidence accepted. The Court relied on the medical jurist's time-of-death opinion (PW-17), PW-6's account contradicting PW-1, the rain evidence, the absence of the Daily Diary entry, and the post-investigation nature of the FIR to discredit the prosecution case
witness_credibility: PW-1 (complainant, claimed eyewitness) held wholly unreliable; PW-6's evidence contradicted PW-1's claim to have witnessed the incident; PW-27 failed to prove disclosure and seizure memos
post_offence_conduct: Not stated for the accused; the Court noted that family members and villagers left the body unprotected overnight
bail_history: Accused were on bail at the Supreme Court stage; bail bonds discharged. Earlier bail history not stated
trial_duration: offence: 19 September 2001 (as alleged); trial judgment: 23 July 2005; High Court: 14 September 2009; Supreme Court: 19 April 2024
legal_representation: Accused: Basavaprabhu S. Patil, Sr. Adv., with Geet Ahuja, Anirudh Sanganeria, Samarth Kashyap and Aman Banka. State: Aman Panwar, A.A.G., with V. N. Raghupathy, Manendra Pal Gupta, Shivam Singh Baghal and Harsh Gattani
investigation_status: FIR registered (Ex P-10) on the complaint; investigation concluded; charge sheet filed; case committed to Sessions; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Daily Diary entry not produced; contradiction on whether the complaint was written at the police station or recorded at the complainant's home; FIR held to be a post-investigation document; disclosure and seizure memos not proved by PW-27; no serological opinion obtained
appeal_history: Trial court: all accused acquitted (23 July 2005). High Court: State's appeal allowed in part; A-1 to A-3 convicted under s.302 r/w s.34 IPC (14 September 2009). Supreme Court: appeal by A-1 to A-3 allowed; High Court judgment reversed and acquittal restored
prosecution_argument: The State argued that the High Court re-appreciated the evidence and rightly found the eyewitnesses (PW-1, PW-2, PW-4, PW-6, PW-15) convincing; the FIR was promptly lodged; the trial court's contradictions were trivial and its acquittal perverse
defence_argument: The High Court reversed acquittal without finding perversity or misreading, and re-appreciated evidence as a first court; eyewitnesses did not act as eyewitnesses would; the FIR was post-investigation; the complainant was shown the weapons on the day of the incident; the disclosure statements and recovery memos were unsigned by the accused
legal_principle_applied: Appeal against acquittal may be allowed only where the acquittal suffers from patent perversity, misreading or omission to consider material evidence, or where only the view consistent with guilt is possible; the appellate court must record pertinent findings on these factors. Statements under Evidence Act s.27 are admissible only to the extent they lead to discovery, and the investigating officer must narrate the conversation; the Evidence Act s.60 requires direct oral evidence
precedent_relied_upon: Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar [2022] 3 SCR 1046 : (2022) 3 SCC 471; H.D. Sundara v. State of Karnataka [2023] 14 SCR 47 : (2023) 9 SCC 581; Mohd. Abdul Hafeez v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1983) 1 SCC 143; Subramanya v. State of Karnataka [2022] 14 SCR 828 : 2022 SCC Online SC 1400 (relied on). Referred to: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Deoman Upadhyaya [1961] 1 SCR 14 : AIR 1960 SC 1125; Ramanand @ Nandlal Bharti v. State of Uttar Pradesh [2022] 5 SCR 162 : 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1396
other_sentence_order: Bail bonds discharged; accused need not surrender
